title: The king who stayed king
hook: a king hears the sage Yajnavalkya say the knower's body lies like a snake's old skin. then he goes on ruling
carry: jivanmukti: free while still living in the body

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana and Nachiketa: moksha isn't earned; it's what the self already is.

King Janaka of Videha loves hard questions, and his court is famous for them. When the sage Yajnavalkya visits, the king keeps him talking, about dreams, about deep sleep, about what happens at death, and again and again he says: I'll give you a thousand cows, sir; teach me more, for freedom. So Yajnavalkya describes the one who has let go of every desire in the heart. Such a person, he says, reaches Brahman here, in this life. And he gives a picture. As a snake's cast-off skin lies on an anthill, dead and thrown away, so lies this body. The shape is still there; the snake has moved on. Janaka didn't leave his throne. Hindus remember him as the king who knew the self and kept ruling; the Bhagavad Gita names him among those who reached perfection through action.
screen: `A KING WHO LOVES QUESTIONS.` → `A THOUSAND COWS: TEACH ME MORE.` → `A SKIN ON AN ANTHILL.`

segments.voice: Shankara reaches for this skin near the end of his comment on the Brahma Sutra's fourth line, the last of the four lines we've followed this week. One, the wish to know Brahman. Two, that from which this world comes. Three, the source of scripture. Four, the texts all connect in it. Then the image. Being embodied, Shankara says, comes from the old mix-up, the I taken for the body. When knowing removes the mix-up, the body doesn't vanish. It goes on walking, eating, getting tired. But it's no longer taken for the self. Like the skin on the anthill, it keeps its shape, and nobody is trapped inside it. Advaita teachers call this jivanmukti, freedom while still living. And Shankara adds a test that's hard to forget: someone who has truly understood doesn't live in the turning world the way they did before; someone who still does hasn't understood yet. Many seekers renounce everything, as Shankara himself did; for many Hindus, Janaka shows the knowing doesn't need a cave. Today we're told to find ourselves in our roles: the job, the grades, the image. This teaching says you can carry every role and be held by none.
screen: `A WISH, A POINTER, A SOURCE, A HARMONY.` · `THE BODY NO LONGER TAKEN FOR THE SELF.` · `JIVANMUKTI: FREE WHILE LIVING.` · `EVERY ROLE, HELD BY NONE.`

segments.voice: Feel the whole body sitting, from the soles of the feet to the top of the head, and let the chair or the floor carry its weight. Then name, quietly, the roles you'll carry today: student, child, friend, worker. Hold each one lightly, like a skin with nobody trapped inside. If you pray, offer the day's roles; if you don't, simply rest.
Jnana. Knowing. For Shankara, the knowing that removes the mix-up and changes where you stand, as a snake leaves its skin behind.
Your line: jivanmukti: free while still living in the body. Janaka kept his throne. Back tomorrow, same hill.
